entries.title: Nationals 8, Cardinals 5: Game Recap
entries.summary: Nats score four runs in the 11th inning to earn the victory.
entries.content:
ST. LOUIS — Washington successfully challenged for catcher’s interference with the bases loaded in a four-run 11th inning in the Nationals’ 8-5 victory over the St. Louis Cardinals on Saturday night.

After Washington took the lead on the interference call, Jose Tena had a two-run double and Dylan Crews followed with an RBI sacrifice fly.

J.J. Wetherholt led off the bottom of the 11th with an RBI single, and St. Louis loaded the bases with no outs, but did not score again. Washington reliever Will Dion got the final out for his first career save.

Riley Cornelio (3-2) was the winner. Gordon Graceffo (8-2) took the loss.

The Nationals (73-82) have won six of their last seven following a seven-game losing streak. The Cardinals (75-80) have lost four straight games.

Jorbit Vivas had a career-high four hits and added an RBI and a run for Washington. James Wood had two hits and scored a run. Daylen Lile blasted a two-run home run to center field in the first inning, the 22nd of the season for the 23-year-old left fielder.

Nathan Church led off the bottom of the ninth with an infield hit that bounced off the second base bag for a double. Pedro Pages followed with an RBI single to left, his first RBI since June 18, to tie it at 3.

Vivas hit a two-out RBI single in the 10th inning to give the Nationals a 4-3 lead, only for Mason Wynn to tie it with an RBI single in the bottom of the inning.
entries.author: Associated Press

entries.title: Virginia Tech 35, Maryland 26: Game Recap
entries.summary: Ethan Grunkemeyer threw for three touchdowns as the Hokies snapped the Terrapins' 20-game nonconference winning streak.
entries.content:
Ethan Grunkemeyer threw for 314 yards and three touchdowns, and Virginia Tech held off Maryland 35-26 on Saturday night, snapping the Terrapins' 20-game nonconference winning streak.

It was the first test against a Power Four opponent for the Hokies (3-0) under new coach James Franklin, and they led from the start. Virginia Tech scored touchdowns on five of its first six possessions, taking a 35-14 advantage into the fourth quarter.

Maryland's nonconference winning streak was the longest in the Football Bowl Subdivision. That now belongs to BYU at 16 games.

“We're fortunate to get out of here with a win,” Franklin said. “I thought we played really good complementary football.”

Maryland's Malik Washington threw for 359 yards and three touchdowns, but a pair of missed 2-point conversions in the fourth kept the Terrapins (2-1) from pulling within one score.

Grunkemeyer opened the scoring with a 14-yard touchdown pass to Luke Reynolds on the game's first possession. Then on third-and-goal from the 18, Grunkemeyer was able to escape the pocket and run for a TD.

Iverson Howard scored on a 2-yard run for Maryland, but a 49-yard catch-and-run touchdown by Virginia Tech's Jeffrey Overton Jr. made it 20-7 with 9:14 left in the half.

Washington threw a 12-yard touchdown pass to Chris Durr Jr. with 2:11 remaining in the second quarter, only for the Hokies to march 75 yards for a touchdown. Grunkemeyer's 2-yard pass to Ja'Ricous Hairston made it 27-14 at the half.

Virginia Tech went 8 of 9 on third down and gained 302 total yards in the half.

Overton scored on a 2-yard run in the third quarter. Washington threw scoring passes of 2 yards to Dorian Fleming and 13 yards to Durr in the fourth.

entries.title: Ted Leonsis Discusses Contracts for Jagr and Ovechkin in New Book
entries.summary: In conversation with Orioles owner David Rubenstein, Leonsis details a big early mistake and a call from the NBA’s David Stern.
entries.content:
Ted Leonsis is giving fans a peek at his life as a sports owner in an interview for a new book, including details on a pair of high-profile contracts.

The 69-year-old owner of the Capitals, Mystics and Wizards is part of an upcoming book by Orioles owner David Rubenstein titled, “Inside the Owner’s Box: Conversations on Power and Leadership in Sports.” The book comes out Tuesday and includes conversations with several team owners, as Rubenstein attempts to make sense of the profession.

In the book, Leonsis, who bought the Capitals in 1999, expressed regret over how he handled the team’s pursuit of Jaromir Jagr in 2001. The Capitals signed Jagr to a seven-year, $77 million deal, which was the largest contract in NHL history at the time, after his 11-year run with the Penguins, which included two Stanley Cups. Both Jagr and the Capitals failed to live up to expectations, and the team traded him to the Rangers in 2004 while continuing to pay part of his salary.

It was an early lesson in ownership for Leonsis.

“I advocated maybe a little more enthusiastically than I should have,” Leonsis said to Rubenstein in the book. “We brought Jaromir here, and that was a disaster. I made a mistake.”

But Leonsis also goes into some of his success stories. In 2008, Capitals executive Dick Patrick convinced Leonsis to give Alex Ovechkin a 13-year contract. At the time, the Capitals star was in the final year of his rookie deal. Ovechkin went on to become one of the league’s greatest players.

Ovechkin’s contract led then-NBA commissioner David Stern to call Leonsis and offer his two cents.

“Thirteen years is the stupidest thing I’ve ever heard,” Stern said, according to Leonsis, who added that his only regret was he didn’t add more years to the deal.

Did Stern ever admit to Leonsis he was wrong?

“No, but they changed the rules, so you can’t give deals like that anymore,” Leonsis told Rubenstein.

On Wednesday, the NHL collective bargaining agreement changed to make deals even shorter, from eight years to seven. Perhaps drawing from previous experience, Leonsis and the Capitals signed two second-year players to eight-year extensions just before the deadline changed.

entries.title: Trump Will Meet With Mamdani in New York
entries.summary: The president and foreign leaders will be in New York this week for the U.N. General Assembly.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump will meet with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Monday, as the president travels to the city for the United Nations General Assembly this week.

The meeting marks the third time Trump and Mamdani have met in person. The pair will sit down at Gracie Mansion, the mayor’s official residence.

“The meeting will focus on issues affecting New York City and New Yorkers,” Mamdani’s office said in a statement. The White House also confirmed the meeting.

Trump and Mamdani have a complex relationship. The president sharply criticized Mamdani during his campaign for mayor, calling him a “a 100% Communist Lunatic” in a post on Truth Social in June 2025.

But after Mamdani visited the Oval Office in November 2025, Trump appeared to change his tune on the mayor and said he “ran an incredible race” and is “a very rational person.”
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: ‘They Better Behave’: Trump Weighs Next Move on Iran
entries.summary: The president said he is in “deciding mode” and “very big things” will happen soon.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump cut his weekend trip to Camp David short and returned to the White House as tensions mount with the war in Iran and across the Middle East.

Trump told Fox News’ Trey Yingst on Sunday that he is in “deciding mode” and warned that "very big things" may happen soon regarding the U.S.-Iran war.

"My question is, if and when do I blow the entire nation up? They better behave," Trump said, according to Fox News.

Iran sent a list of conditions for ending the war to the U.S. through Qatari mediators, and Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told Al Jazeera on Saturday that the country is awaiting Trump’s response.

The president traveled to his golf club in Sterling, Virginia, on Sunday morning.

Trump told Fox News he is considering three options: “wiping Iran out,” “letting them rot economically” or “making a deal.” Trump also said he is “open” to meeting with Iran’s president Masoud Pezeshkian during the United Nations General Assembly meeting this week.

The State Department also warned Americans in the Middle East to stay on alert, saying the “military conflict has the potential to escalate rapidly.”

“Due to tensions in the Middle East, the security environment remains complex with the potential for unforeseen escalation,” the State Department wrote in the alert. “Americans currently in the Middle East should exercise heightened vigilance and be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions.”

The notice pointed to the Iran-backed Houthi rebels attacking a civilian airport in Saudi Arabia, which is a U.S. ally in the region. Trump told Fox News he remains in constant communication with the Houthis and they have agreed not to fight the U.S.

Saudi Arabia said Saturday that they intercepted the ballistic missile the Houthis launched at the capital city Riyadh, and large plumes of smoke could be seen at the city’s main airport.

U.S. embassies and missions in Israel, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Kuwait, Lebanon, Jordan, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar all issued warnings about the security threat over the weekend.

Trump’s comments on the war follow statements he made to Axios on Friday about approaching a “big decision” about whether to potentially go “in and annihilate them [the Iranian regime]” or not.

entries.title: Trump Says His Planned Arch Would Also Become a 'Military Complex'
entries.summary: The president said the proposed arch would host drones and snipers.
entries.content:
By Seung Min Kim

President Donald Trump said Sunday that the massive arch he wants to build between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery would become a “top grade Military Complex” able to host drones and snipers while storing ammunition.

It is one more example of how Trump is insisting that his initiatives to beautify the White House and D.C. are also serving a defensive purpose. Trump has been calling the new White House ballroom a “military complex” and arguing it is necessary for national security purposes.

The Pentagon said it had no information beyond the president’s statement.

Trump’s announcement also comes as the arch, like his other projects, faces legal challenges. Though the arch has received early approval from the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts, whose members were all tapped by Trump, a group of three veterans and an architectural historian sued, saying the project needs to be approved by Congress.

“The President’s belated efforts to manufacture a national security justification for this project do nothing to cure its fundamental illegality,” Nicolas Sansone, one of the attorneys representing the litigants, said Sunday. “Congress has not authorized the arch and unless and until Congress does so, the project should not be permitted to move forward.”

The president said in a social media post that he had agreed, at the “strong request” of the military, to convert the planned 250-foot-tall memorial arch “into a top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch, to house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage.”

The arch is proposed for a circle adjacent to the Memorial Bridge, which is a heavy-traffic area as one of a handful of connecting bridges between the nation’s capital and Northern Virginia.

Rep. Don Beyer, a Virginia Democrat who represents a district that includes Arlington County and the cities of Alexandria and Falls Church, called out the potential dangers of Trump’s plan given the arch’s proximity to Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport. “Putting a drone launching site directly in the landing path for DCA is a stupid, dangerous, and unworkable idea,” Beyer wrote Sunday on X. “Trump clearly expects to lose a lawsuit and therefore wants to set up a pretext to argue that the arch is tied to national security. Which is obviously idiotic.”

The project is one of several projects that the Republican president is pursuing to leave his lasting imprint on Washington. Among the others are the White House ballroom, renaming and renovating the Kennedy Center, refurbishing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and rebuilding a golf course in East Potomac Park that could significantly reduce the public’s access to running and biking paths.

The groundbreaking for the arch was to have happened sometime this month. The project has not yet received final approval from the National Capital Area Planning Commission, which greenlit the site and preliminary plans at its July meeting. The commission is expected to take up the matter again this fall.

This story has been updated to include comment from an attorney representing a group of people suing over the arch and Rep. Don Beyer’s post.
